items.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank
items.summary: De Cos will lead the ECB into a period of political uncertainty and choppy growth, after winning the backing needed to succeed Christine Lagarde next year.
items.body: Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year. He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit, multiple media reported on Thursday. The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term. Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources. De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.

items.title: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
items.summary: Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time in 2026, as the AI boom fueled chip demand.
items.body: The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data . Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline. Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday.

items.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
items.summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
items.body: There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week. Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations. "We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC. Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda. The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation.

items.title: 430,000 UK homeowners face £500-plus jump in monthly mortgage payments
items.summary: Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise Business live – latest updates More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising…
items.body: More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said. The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments. For about 3.4 million borrowers the monthly increase would be less than £100, while for a further 2.7 million it would be £100-£500. The increase would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 likely to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500. Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month.

items.title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
items.summary: The agreement offers new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at home?
items.body: As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner. At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week , European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people. The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China . For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains. The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.

items.title: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs, sources say
items.summary: A new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday.
items.body: Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC. It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16. Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information. The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19.

items.title: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
items.summary: The U.S. planned a fresh tariff salvo on 14 trading partners, while offering some countries lower rates if they secure trade deals with Washington.
items.body: The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington. The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam. The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington. The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.

items.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
items.summary: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated.
items.body: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show. About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals. That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July. In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments. For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

items.title: Marlboro maker Altria considering takeover bid for Imperial Brands
items.summary: Shares in UK tobacco company jump by more than 14% on news US rival is looking into making offer Business live – latest updates Imperial Brands could become the next UK company to fall to a foreign takeover after its US rival Altria announced a possible bid for the tobacco firm.…
items.body: Imperial Brands could become the next UK company to fall to a foreign takeover after its US rival Altria announced a possible bid for the tobacco firm. Altria, whose Philip Morris division makes Marlboro and Benson & Hedges cigarettes, told the City on Thursday that it was considering an offer. If made it was likely to be solely in cash, it said. Altria also said it was in discussions with a third party about its possible acquisition of part of Imperial Brands’ business, suggesting the company could be broken up. Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until 5pm on 24 December to either announce a firm intention to make an offer or walk away. Imperial responded by saying it had not had any discussions “or received any approach or proposal from Altria or the third party referenced”.

items.title: Simon Jack: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
items.summary: Poundland's management and MPs blame the retailer's owners, Gordon Brothers, but the US firm says without them the chain would have collapsed last year.
items.body: The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already. Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part. The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period. They point to improving sales over recent months as proof the business had a future. MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".

items.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos wins race to be next ECB president
items.summary: Former Bank of Spain governor chosen to succeed Christine Lagarde after winning support of EU’s biggest countries Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s…
items.body: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank , to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries. The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank. EU diplomats agreed two other appointments to the ECB’s executive board on Thursday: France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier. The trio of appointments was a package deal, after France and Germany converged on choosing Hernández de Cos, who is expected to keep the ECB on the same path.

items.title: Trump, NATO chief caution Russia as attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure intensify
items.summary: Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and called for a rapid peaceful resolution.
items.body: U.S. President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte issued a joint statement on Thursday urging Russia not to take any actions, intentionally or otherwise, that would further expand the Ukraine war. The statement comes as Ukraine's allies sound the alarm over Russia's growing threat to European security and just one week after Trump's historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Asia. Trump and Rutte described their meeting at the Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida on Wednesday as "very impactful," with Russia's nearly five-year-long war in Ukraine and the Iran war among the key topics of conversation.

items.title: New boss appointed to lead Travelodge
items.summary: The new CEO will lead the Thame-based company from 1 December following Jo Boydell's resignation.
items.body: Travelodge has appointed a former Tui executive to become its new boss from the start of December. The former CEO of the Oxfordshire-based budget hotel chain Jo Boydell quit in the summer after safety issues were raised at many of its sites. A woman staying at its Maidenhead hotel was sexually assaulted in December 2022 after a man lied to staff to get a key card to her room. Kyran Smith was jailed for seven-and-a-half years for the attack . Peter Krueger will start his new role at Travelodge on Tuesday, replacing interim chief Ray Reidy who has led the company since Boydell quit. She left the company after facing significant criticism over the handling of the sexual assault incident and wider safety concerns. It prompted former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to urge her to "seriously engage" with the government on the issue after she cancelled a meeting with MPs.

items.title: Ministers have ‘failed to make the case’ for Heathrow third runway, MPs say
items.summary: Transport committee says policy papers show expanding airport would fall short of pledges on economy and climate Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at Heathrow , according to a damning report by MPs. The Commons transport committee said on Thursday that…
items.body: Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at Heathrow , according to a damning report by MPs. The Commons transport committee said on Thursday that the detailed policy papers laid out by the government showed expansion of the London airport would fall short of pledges on the economy and climate. The chair of the committee, Ruth Cadbury, said plans for the third runway “should be grounded” and the government needed to “go back to the drawing board”. Heathrow’s owner is seeking to build a third runway and expand its terminals at a cost of about £33bn. It says its plan would almost double passengers numbers and add up to 276,000 flights a year. The committee was tasked with examining the government’s Heathrow expansion national policy statement (HENPS) – but Cadbury said there was a “complete disjoint” between the plans and a lack of wider aviation strategy.

items.body: Texture-maxxing is the latest food trend taking social media by storm as consumers, driven by aesthetics and taste, look for a sensory experience. British supermarket Waitrose's latest food and drink report highlighted "texture-maxxing" as one of the trends of the year. It describes the phenomenon as a multi-sensory indulgence that is "fuelled by texture-maxxing crunch and intense flavour hits," pushing shoppers to fill their trolleys with crunchy peanut butter, dumplings, and trifles. "This year, the sound of food went mainstream," Waitrose's Senior Development Chef Will Torrent said in the Wednesday report.

items.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
items.summary: Why is Poundland closing down, and what will happen to staff and suppliers?
items.body: Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas. The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company. Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it. Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome. When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

items.title: Labour’s split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs
items.summary: Exclusive: Frontbenchers join scores of party colleagues urging Burnham not to let ministers approve project Opinion: Why Labour MPs are opposing Rosebank Podcast: are resignations next? Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open,…
items.body: Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs – including a handful of frontbenchers – writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project. Ninety-two backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers have signed a letter to Andy Burnham urging him not to let his ministers approve the scheme for the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters. It is the clearest sign yet of the deep rift the issue has caused within the Labour party. The chancellor, John Healey, and many Scottish MPs are pushing for it to go ahead , while dozens of others argue for it to be rejected on climate grounds. Feelings are running so high that more than one frontbench ministerial aide is considering resigning if the project is approved, the Guardian has been told.

items.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
items.summary: US company Fender is in dispute with a German firm that makes generic versions of its key model.
items.body: Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments. The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments. The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria. In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars. Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.

items.title: Major East Midlands road projects shelved to divert funding to defence
items.summary: Regional mayor says cancelling works on A38 at Derby and Newark bypass on A46 ‘disappointing and short-sighted’ Two long-awaited major road schemes have been cancelled to divert more than £400m into defence spending, the government has confirmed. Upgrades to roundabouts on the…
items.body: Two long-awaited major road schemes have been cancelled to divert more than £400m into defence spending, the government has confirmed. Upgrades to roundabouts on the A38 around Derby and to the Newark bypass on the A46 will be shelved. Environmental campaigners welcomed the decision but some in the East Midlands who had hoped local bottlenecks would be eased greeting it with dismay. The regional mayor, Labour’s Claire Ward, said the cancellations were disappointing and short-sighted. The projects had been approved and included in the government’s latest roads investment strategy, published in March.

items.title: Switzerland’s biggest bank set for showdown with lawmakers as capital fight intensifies amid crisis planning
items.summary: Swiss regulator FINMA said UBS can execute its preferred crisis-resolution strategy, even as the bank faces a separate parliamentary fight over tougher capital requirements.
items.body: UBS 's crisis planning has won qualified support from market regulators, which called its plan "executable" in principle. But Switzerland's biggest bank still faces a major fight over sweeping plans that would force it to hold more capital against its foreign subsidiaries. FINMA, the Swiss markets regulator, said Wednesday that UBS's resolvability — or its ability to fail safely, without wreaking havoc on the economy — has improved since it integrated rival Credit Suisse, with progress made in implementing the emergency plan across group-wide resolution planning. The preferred resolution strategy — involving plans to allow for recapitalization and restructuring through the use of loss-absorbing bail-in bonds — is "executable," FINMA said. The regulator formally approved UBS's recovery plan for the first time since its ​Credit Suisse integration.

items.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
items.summary: The carrier is looking for urgent funding, but will file for bankruptcy without a financial lifeline.
items.body: The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation. The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo. Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket. One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening. The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic. PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night. In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

items.title: Public service broadcaster services should be top of TV app menus – Ofcom
items.summary: UK regulator’s code of practice on streaming platforms is intended to give prominence to iPlayer and similar offerings Public service broadcasters’ streaming services such as BBC iPlayer should appear first on app menus on smart TVs to give them an “appropriate degree of…
items.body: Public service broadcasters’ streaming services such as BBC iPlayer should appear first on app menus on smart TVs to give them an “appropriate degree of prominence”, according to Ofcom . In addition, the regulator has said public service shows should rank higher on voice and text searches on televisions connected to the internet. In an increasingly fragmented media world, TV guides and app menus act as gatekeepers to content and vary according to which set viewers have, with users often having to scroll for some time to find the traditional broadcasters. So as part of the 2024 Media Act – which modernised the framework for making public service broadcasting content easier to discover on connected TVs – Ofcom has announced a new code of practice that it hopes will help audiences locate PSB shows more easily and standardise prominence on TV screens.

items.title: SpaceX, Musk pledge to donate a share each to active Trump Accounts
items.summary: SpaceX said it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account, and CEO Elon Musk would match it.
items.body: SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account , and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift. "SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit." The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active. Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added.

items.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
items.summary: The changes could see drivers over 70 stripped of licences if they do not meet standards.
items.body: Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans. Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks. Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over. To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required. Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence. The change follows a consultation which launched early last year , set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

items.title: Number of Neets in UK falls below a million as Burnham pushes to tackle crisis
items.summary: Latest figure of young people not in education, employment or training remains close to highest level in a decade Business live – latest updates UK politics live – latest updates The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) has…
items.body: The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) has decreased but remains close to a million as Andy Burnham’s government pushes to tackle Britain’s youth jobs crisis. As ministers prepare to make sweeping changes in response to Alan Milburn’s landmark report on young people and work, the Office for National Statistics said the number of Neets fell by 22,000 in the three months to September, to 959,000. On an annual basis, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not earning or learning was 17,000 higher than a year ago. Although down from a peak of just over a million in March, the latest figure remains close to the highest level in a decade. The prime minister last week promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people after Milburn said Britain risked “losing a generation of young people” without a radical change in course.

items.title: Inside India newsletter: Roaring economy, foreign investors’ return and now record auto sales
items.summary: Automakers in India are poised to sell over 30 million vehicles in the financial year ending March 2027.
items.body: Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. Despite 2026 being a challenging year with high global energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the Indian economy has fared surprisingly well. The auto industry, a key pillar of manufacturing and employment, has breached several records this year and is poised to report its best-ever sales. This week, I spoke to experts to decode what this stellar performance means for one of the world's most promising consumer markets. India's economy expanded at 7.8% in the June quarter, beating expectations, even as growth in several major economies cooled. Foreign portfolio investors who had been exiting Indian markets in droves for most of the year have also started returning in historic numbers.

items.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
items.summary: Text of the treaties was published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
items.body: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset. The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal. The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal. Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay. The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship. The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

items.title: Mandelson tried to set up meeting between Trump adviser and lobbying firm he held shares in
items.summary: Then ambassador to US wanted to discuss alternatives to World Trade Organization in ‘under the radar’ meeting, documents reveal Peter Mandelson sought to organise an “under the radar” meeting between a member of his former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, and an economic adviser…
items.body: Peter Mandelson sought to organise an “under the radar” meeting between a member of his former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, and an economic adviser to Donald Trump, while he still held shares in the company, newly released documents reveal. Mandelson’s attempt to organise the meeting followed a Foreign Office proposal of a “light-touch way” to protect him “against perceptions of benefiting [Global Counsel] in some way while in public office”. In April 2025, while ambassador to Washington, Mandelson wanted to hold a lunch to discuss “alternative options” to the World Trade Organization and on how “like-minded partners come to terms with China and its practices”. He told the economic adviser he wanted to bring “a former trade colleague of mine” with “interesting views” who could “lead off”.

items.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights, warns it may file for bankruptcy after share price collapse
items.summary: Norse Atlantic has suspended all flights and said it may it have to file for bankruptcy, a day after it warned its financial position was "critical."
items.body: Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation. "The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse said in a Thursday statement. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy." The airline added that "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found." Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets for flights on Friday and beyond as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday. Warning signs first popped up when PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.

items.title: China made Shenzhen a showcase for tech prowess at APEC summit
items.body: I just came back from Shenzhen, after covering the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit . Based on its track record, the Chinese leadership's intention in choosing the country's tech hub to host APEC was quite clear to me. When China had the chance to host the gathering for the first time in 2001, it selected Shanghai. After being admitted to join the multilateral club mainly by liberal democracies in 1991, alongside Taiwan and Hong Kong, China was desperate to crawl out from international isolation and sanctions over the killing of unarmed students and citizens on June 4, 1989 , in and around Tiananmen Square in the heart of its capital, Beijing.

items.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
items.summary: Millions could be entitled to compensation as a result of commission arrangements between lenders and dealers.
items.body: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements could face further delays to compensation after the financial regulator said it had made some errors in its calculations. Driver have already been told they must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.

items.title: Some old-school advice for Burnham: boost competition if you want growth | Nils Pratley
items.summary: Two former Treasury officials say the value of competition and disruption has become ‘the blind spot of UK economic policy’ The defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should…
items.body: T he defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government. Bokkerink was chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) until he was turfed out because, it seemed, he was deemed insufficiently aligned with the Starmer-Reeves idea that regulators should “support growth”. Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”. The exchange pointed to a philosophical divide.

items.title: ‘Your booth is waiting’: Denny’s welcomes Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
items.summary: Denny's reaffirmed its longstanding ties with Jensen Huang following his return as Nvidia CEO, revealing that a plaque had been restored.
items.body: Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him. The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13. "Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X . The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993. The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed. "We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.

items.title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee
items.summary: High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1 When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north…
items.body: W hen the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.” They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.” He was told that day to keep the shop looking neat (“As I always do”), but more shelves are bare, the Christmas glitz a mockery to those fearing they’ll have no job by then. Now he is worrying about pay. “They paid us early this week and I don’t know why.

items.title: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
items.summary: Nvidia GPU sellers are seeking new buyers after new U.S. rules tightened remote access to advanced AI chips for China-linked customers
items.body: Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems. Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said. Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.

items.title: 36% minimum wage hike tests Bangladesh garment sector's low-cost model
items.body: DHAKA -- Bangladesh's move to raise the minimum monthly wage for garment workers by 36% after several weeks of protests marks a significant adjustment for an industry that is a major employer and exporter but has long relied on a low-cost model.

items.title: I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why | Catherine Fookes
items.summary: Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs This week it was…
items.body: This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills , just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK . The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains. This is why I, along with my colleagues on Labour’s backbenches, have written to the prime minister urging that his government makes the right decision and rejects the Rosebank oilfield .

items.title: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test
items.summary: Latin America’s copper, oil, gas and rare earths could benefit from rising AI energy demand, if infrastructure and fiscal policy attract investment.
items.body: Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials. But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects. "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added. Ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers.

items.title: Wife of Japanese journalist held in Russia pleads for his release
items.body: TOKYO -- The wife of a Japanese journalist held in Russia pleaded for his return on Thursday in her first public statement since her husband's detention more than a month ago. "Please return this precious papa to his little daughter," wrote Nozomi Imai, who is married to Yuki Imai, a Hokkaido Shimbun reporter. "He is a beloved son, husband, and father." Imai was detained by Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) on Oct. 13, just one day before he was due to return to Japan after completing a two-year assignment in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, a city on the island of Sakhalin in Russia's Far East. His wife recounted her reaction to a video released by Russian authorities showing her husband being taken away. "I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart," she wrote.

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly…
items.body: I ’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people. We are encouraged to see ourselves as though we are in a race not just against other companies and even against entire countries, but also against other teams within our own company.

items.title: Wealthy Europeans look beyond stocks amid AI selloff. Here’s where they’re investing
items.summary: Goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth investors found they're increasingly looking to alternatives amid turbulent markets.
items.body: Wealthy Europeans are looking to alternative asset classes to build exposure to artificial intelligence themes amid turbulence in public markets. Goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S. investors. The survey found a significant gap between the U.S. and Europe in terms of investor knowledge of alternatives, which include assets like private equity, property and infrastructure. Goldman said 82% of European respondents are familiar with the alternative investments market — compared to 50% of U.S. investors. Goldman polled 1,000 investors with at least 1 million in investable assets in their local currency across the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland.

items.body: TOKONAME, Japan -- Automotive and robotics companies are facing a reality check in central Japan's Aichi prefecture, home to Toyota Motor, as they seek to turn a combination of humanoids and physical AI into practical applications for the vehicle industry.

items.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
items.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
items.body: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy". However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky. There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.

items.title: Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can attack other energy costs more ruthlessly
items.summary: Louise Haigh talked the right talk at the CBI this week, but greater ambition and tighter timelines are needed Shocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the…
items.body: S hocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027. Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz. But EDF’s outlook for next year currently reads: £2,254 for the second quarter, which will include about £100 extra in the “network costs” line in bills that includes paying for the upgrade of the electricity grid – demonstrating that gas prices are not the only story on a medium and long-term horizon. Then £2,078 in the quarter starting in July and £2,035 from October.

items.title: Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk
items.summary: The 20,000-square-meter mega factory will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, making it the world's third-largest satellite production site.
items.body: The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S. space infrastructure. Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX 's Starlink business. Aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov. 30. Its new oval-shaped, 20,000-square-meter facility in southern Belgium, inaugurated by Belgian King Philippe, will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, which would make it the world's third-largest satellite production site, according to the Belgian royal palace.

items.body: ISLAMABAD -- Since U.S. President Donald Trump began his second term in office in January last year, the country's economic ties with Pakistan have deepened significantly, sharply boosting bilateral trade. items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this…
items.body: A sk Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. Mr Burnham correctly identified the transmission mechanism by which geopolitical problems feed domestic political resentment.

items.title: S&P warns Nvidia credit rating could be cut over 'rising' management and governance risk
items.summary: S&P Global Ratings said Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch as it flagged "rising" management and governance risk at the chipmaker.
items.body: Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. "News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note . S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed. A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs.

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.summary: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine…
items.body: W hen I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain.

items.summary: Proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, offer India a competitive advantage.
items.body: The latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if New Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal. The Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if New Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests. Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters. The U.S.

items.title: Employers: do you have concerns about the rollout of Muse and other AI agents?
items.summary: Are you worried about staff connecting their digital assistants to work emails and databases? What steps are you taking to address this? Meta has rolled out its Muse AI assistant, which can be tasked with shopping, booking tickets and carrying out negotiations on a user’s…
items.body: Are you worried about staff connecting their digital assistants to work emails and databases? What steps are you taking to address this? Meta has rolled out its Muse AI assistant, which can be tasked with shopping, booking tickets and carrying out negotiations on a user’s behalf, across countries including the UK, US, Canada, Australia and Japan. The AI agent needs the customer’s permission to go out and make purchases, connect to apps, use bank details or send emails autonomously. However, the possibility of employees connecting their Muse assistant to their work emails and databases is a concern for companies and their clients. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office says firms using agentic AI “must be able to demonstrate how they comply with UK data protection law on an ongoing basis, including by identifying … steps to mitigate risks of harm to users and the wider public”.

items.title: North Korea's Kim calls for nuclear arsenal expansion, says status 'will never change'
items.summary: Kim Jong Un called for wider use of tactical nuclear weapons and an expanded arsenal, rejecting international denuclearization pressure.
items.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for bolstering the country's nuclear arsenal and expanding the use of tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains, state media reported Thursday, as Pyongyang reaffirmed its determination to retain its nuclear arms. Kim's comments followed a working visit Wednesday to facilities involved in nuclear material production and weapons research, according to the Korean Central News Agency. At the Nuclear Weapons Institute, he urged greater attention to "operationalizing" tactical nuclear weapons for a range of missions. Kim directly linked the development of those weapons to North Korea "sharing a border with its most dangerous, hostile state," an apparent reference to South Korea.

items.title: Cost of living roadshow highlights support on offer
items.summary: This event in Sheerness is funded by the Crisis and Resilience Fund for those facing cash issues.
items.body: A cost of living roadshow held in a Kent town is the "starting point" and "first step on the ladder" to resolve financial problems, a local councillor has said. Organisations, including those which help people with health and wellbeing, managing bills and getting back into work, have been in Sheerness for the Swale Borough Council event on Thursday morning. Councillor Angela Harrison, deputy mayor of Swale, wants residents to know that "there is help support and guidance for you". Among those in attendance was Nichola Hermitage from Positively Connected Kent, which helps people manage energy costs and fuel debt. Reacting to the recent announcement that energy prices are due to go up by 26% in January, Hermitage said there were small measures people can take to mitigate the impact.

items.title: Ministry of Defence signs £8.7bn deal with Babcock to maintain submarines
items.summary: Wes Streeting says deal will ‘get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster’ amid scrutiny of nuclear deterrent UK politics live – latest updates Business live – latest updates The Ministry of Defence has signed an £8.7bn contract with the defence company Babcock to…
items.body: The Ministry of Defence has signed an £8.7bn contract with the defence company Babcock to maintain Britain’s submarine fleet amid scrutiny of the performance of the country’s nuclear deterrent. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting , said the five-year contract would “get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster”. The UK’s four nuclear-armed submarines patrol the oceans to provide a continuous at-sea deterrent, staying submerged to avoid detection and to be able to launch Trident missiles even if land-based weapons are destroyed. However, even as the perceived threats to the UK have increased in recent years, particularly from Russia in the northern Atlantic, the fleet has faced concerns over its readiness after a series of faults forced some of the submarines into dry docks for months at a time.

items.title: Robots could be doing household chores in just 1-2 years, Chinese EV firm says
items.summary: Xpeng Co-President Brian Gu shared his humanoid robot predictions with CNBC in an interview Thursday.
items.body: BEIJING — The household robot could soon become a reality, Brian Gu, co-president of Xpeng , a Chinese electric car company which has entered the humanoids space, told CNBC. "Maybe after successful deployment into commercial settings, maybe another one to two years, we can start thinking about deploying into home settings," Gu said. "Technology is moving at a much faster clip." Xpeng revealed its latest general-purpose humanoid robot Iron on Wednesday. The company plans to start training the robot as a store assistant in its retail car locations in the first quarter next year, after starting mass production in January. Sales are set to begin in the second quarter, with deliveries expected later in the year. Founded in 2014 as an electric car company, Xpeng beat Tesla to rolling out driver-assist in mainland China. The Chinese automaker has launched its own artificial intelligence chips.

items.summary: FCA also tells Barclays to stop making settlement offers while it works through data problems Business live – latest updates The financial regulator has admitted that it has miscalculated part of the compensation scheme for victims of the car finance scandal and told Barclays to…
items.body: The financial regulator has admitted that it has miscalculated part of the compensation scheme for victims of the car finance scandal and told Barclays to stop making settlement offers while it works through the data problems. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) revealed it had identified “some errors in how we categorised a small group of loan agreements’, which will affect the average compensation payout to drivers. The errors were discovered as the FCA prepared its response to a legal challenge against its £9.1bn compensation scheme for drivers overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers. That scheme, announced in March, prompted a legal battle that has forced the regulator to partly suspend it . A hearing to decide what happens is due to go ahead in February.

items.title: K-beauty stocks rally as Korean brands top Amazon bestseller lists globally ahead of Black Friday
items.summary: South Korean beauty stocks rose as K-beauty brands dominated Amazon's skincare rankings ahead of Black Friday.
items.body: South Korean beauty stocks jumped Thursday as the country's skincare brands dominated Amazon's bestseller rankings ahead of Black Friday. Shares of K-beauty giant APR climbed 3.77%, while cosmetic contracts manufacturers Kolmar Korea and Cosmax gained 5.46% and 2.91%, respectively. APR shares, in particular, have rallied sharply this week, up 28%, defying a broader market sell-off in Seoul markets, with the benchmark Kospi index down 2.65% during the same period. A cosmetic sector index tracked by Meritz Securities had gained 12% this week until Wednesday, according to a Thursday note from the brokerage. The rally reflects renewed optimism over earnings growth following strong performances by K-beauty brands across major e-commerce platforms in the U.S.

items.title: Parents cutting basics at Christmas, charity warns
items.summary: The chief executive of Worthing Soup Kitchen says some families choose between food and presents.
items.body: Christmas is likely to see families cut back on essentials to try and meet the expenses of the festive period, a West Sussex soup kitchen has warned. Katrina McCormack, chief executive of the Shout Worthing Soup Kitchen, told BBC Radio Sussex that they are forced to limit the amount of support they can give due to high demand at Christmas, and make sure their shelves are stocked. It comes at the start of a campaign to raise thousands for turkey and other Christmas trimmings for struggling families, which the charity says is a "driving force" for their work in December. McCormack said: "We ran an afternoon tea with Father Christmas, and last year we had children asking him for food." She added: "A lot of families are struggling to pay that extra, they are struggling to put food on the table.

items.title: UK watchdog calls for shake-up of private dentistry market amid ‘catalogue of concerns’
items.summary: CMA report highlights inflation-busting annual rises and practices that ‘may not operate in patients’ best interests’ Tell us: what is your experience of UK private dentistry? Business live – latest updates The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a shake-up of the £8bn…
items.body: The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a shake-up of the £8bn private dentistry market , after an investigation identified a “catalogue of concerns” including inflation-busting annual rises and evidence of targets to sell more expensive treatments and dental payment plans. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said patients faced substantial differences in prices in different parts of the UK and “commercial practices, targets and incentives [that] may not operate in patients’ best interests”. The report found dentists typically had a financial stake in treatment revenues, either as practice owners or through revenue-sharing arrangements. “We have also seen evidence of targets to convert NHS patients to private care, sell more expensive treatments, and increase sales of dental payment plans,” the CMA said.

items.title: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
items.summary: Whether the Trump administration has investigated Jensen Huang for potential national security risks has been the subject of questions.
items.body: Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation. "I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation." Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done. Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws. "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.

items.title: Japan arcade snags world record with 600 claw machines
items.body: TOKYO -- Japanese amusement company Aeon Fantasy opened an arcade Wednesday that holds a world record for the most claw machines in a single location.
